newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya sees 96/97 coffee output below 90,000 tonnes.
newsitem.headline: Kenya sees 96/97 coffee output below 90,000 tonnes.

text.p: Poor weather and disease will cut Kenya's 1996/97 coffee production to below 90,000 tonnes from 97,575 tonnes in 1995/96, coffee authorities said on Wednesday.
Aggrey Ole Murunga, general manager of the Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK), told Reuters "we are now looking at just below 90,000 tonnes for 1996/97 but that figure could go lower".

Murunga blamed coffee berry disease (CBD) in a number of key growing districts as well as poor weather in others for the setback in production. It comes after after a rise in the crop from 75,516 tonnes in 1993/94 to 95,806 tonnes in 1994/95.
"This disease is the problem. It could reduce production further than we already envisage," Murunga told Reuters on the sidelines of the board's annual delegates conference.

Board Chairman John Zachariah Ngari attributed the steady rise in production in the 1993/94 to 1994/95 period to a positive response by farmers in all growing areas as a result of good coffee prices that farmers have enjoyed since 1992/93.
"Farmers have intensified their efforts, we have no problem in that area," Ngari said.
Ngari said coffee quality had showed a slight improvement in the last three years because of better management and prompt payments to farmers. Good quality would be maintained .
Murunga said Kenya would be represented at a special conference of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) in Brazil "but Kenya's position is well-understood".
That position is that with Kenya's auction system, stocks are automatically withheld from the market if prices are not right.

"Our position is well understood by other producers. We do not have to be party to their agreements although we go along. We have an auction system in which stocks are retained if prices are not right. Prices for our coffee are very encouraging," Murunga said.
Simeon Nyachae, agriculture minister until his transfer on Wednesday, has previously said that Kenya's production was too small anyway and made little impact on global supplies.
Murunga's production figures were the fifth revision so far this year. The board first spoke of 100,000 tonnes, then revised the figure to 96,000 tonnes, then 95,000 and then 90,000 tonnes.
Ngari said roads in growing areas were being improved after the government allowed cess, a tax on farmers for infrastructure, to be collected and administered by farmers themselves.
He added that Kenya had low carry-over stocks.

He put exports at 79,482 tonnes worth 14.4 billion shillings ($261.81 million) in 1994/95, rising to 109,372 tonnes worth 16.36 billion shillings in 1995/96. Part of the 1995/96 exports were carry-over stocks from 1994/95.
